*   **Variable Size Access:** Accessing the $i$-th child requires summing the sizes of all preceding pointers $[0, i-1]$.
This differs from SVDAG, which only had sizes 0 and 4.
*   **Precision:** The 13-bit offset in 16-bit pointers limits addressing to the first 16 KB of inner levels and 64 KB of leaf levels.
*   **Transformation Accumulation:** The transformation status is cumulative.
It must be XOR-ed with each pointer's transformation code as the traversal descends.
*   **Memory Footprint:** Significantly reduced compared to fixed-pointer SVDAGs.
The variable-length encoding allows compact storage, improving cache utilization.
Measured performance on specific hardware and exact scaling factors are not given in the sources.
The SSVDAG node layout was introduced by Kämpe et al. in 2016 as an extension of the Sparse Voxel DAG (SVDAG) [Kämpe et al. 2013].
The original SVDAG used fixed 4-byte pointers.
The SSVDAG method was developed to further reduce memory consumption by exploiting the fact that many child pointers are null or point to nearby nodes, allowing for variable-length encoding.
